textTitles: The sand we are running out of

texts.title: The sand we are running out of

paragraphs.text: Sand is the second most heavily used natural resource on earth after water, and almost nobody thinks about it. Fifty billion tonnes of it are dug, dredged and crushed every year, most of it to make concrete, and the rest to make glass, silicon chips and the ground under new roads. The paradox that follows is the reason the subject has become interesting: the planet is covered in deserts, and the world is running short of sand. The grains that lie in the Sahara have been rolled by wind for millions of years until they are round and smooth, and rounded grains will not lock together in concrete. What builders need is angular sand, and angular sand comes from rivers, lakes, floodplains and the sea floor. Those are also the places where removing it does the most harm, which is the whole of the problem in one sentence.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Demand has risen with the cities. A single medium-sized apartment block absorbs several thousand tonnes of sand, a kilometre of motorway roughly thirty thousand, and a large nuclear power station about twelve million. Construction in Asia over the past three decades has used quantities that have no historical precedent; by several estimates, more concrete was poured in China in three years at the start of the 2010s than in the United States during the whole of the twentieth century. Because sand is heavy and cheap, it cannot be shipped far without the transport costing more than the material, so every building boom eats the riverbed nearest to it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The environmental bill arrives downstream. Dredging a river deepens its channel, which lowers the water table on either side and leaves wells and irrigation pumps drawing air. It undercuts bridge piers, and bridges have collapsed as a result. It removes the material that would otherwise be carried to the coast, so deltas that are already sinking receive less of the sediment that keeps them above the sea, and the fields behind them take in salt. Fisheries fail, because the creatures at the bottom of the food chain live in exactly the gravel that the dredger is lifting. None of these costs appears in the price of a tonne of sand, and all of them are paid by somebody.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Where the law is weak, the trade attracts people who are not builders. Illegal extraction is now a substantial criminal business in several countries: boats work at night, officials are paid to look at the river in the morning, and journalists and local officials who ask questions have been threatened and, in a number of documented cases, killed. The economics make it almost inevitable. The raw material is lying in public rivers, the equipment is a barge and a pump, the buyer is a legitimate construction company that asks no questions, and the penalty, where there is one, is a fine smaller than a night’s takings. Enforcement fails less because the law is unclear than because the people who would enforce it live beside the river.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: There are ways to use less of it. Crushed rock from quarries makes acceptable concrete for many purposes, and so does the rubble of demolished buildings once it has been sorted and cleaned, a practice now required on public projects in several European countries. Some mixtures replace part of the sand with ash from coal stations or slag from steelworks. None of this is free: recycled aggregate costs more to prepare than river sand costs to dredge, and the industry moves only when the price gap closes or when a regulator makes it move. The most effective measure is the simplest and the least popular, which is to build less and to build with timber and with what is already standing.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What is missing is arithmetic. Most countries do not know how much sand they extract, because the reporting is voluntary, the informal trade is invisible and satellite monitoring of riverbeds has only recently become cheap enough to use. Until a government knows what leaves its rivers each year it cannot set a limit, price a licence or notice that a delta is starving. The problem is not that sand is scarce in any absolute sense; the planet has plenty of rock and time makes more sand from it. The problem is that we are removing a slow resource at industrial speed, in the places where taking it does the most damage, and we are not counting.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Play is expensive. A young animal at play burns energy it could store, makes noise that a predator can hear, and takes risks that a cautious animal would not: young goats leap off rocks, otters slide down mud banks, and kittens ambush objects that are not going anywhere. Records from several field studies suggest that a small but real fraction of deaths among young mammals happen during play. Behaviour that costs this much and survives in so many species is a puzzle, because natural selection is not sentimental, and biologists have spent a century trying to work out what the animals are buying.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first task is to say what counts. The working definition used in most studies has several parts: the behaviour is not immediately useful, it is performed in a relaxed setting rather than under threat, it is repeated, it is exaggerated or clumsy compared with the serious version, and it is often begun with a signal that announces it is not in earnest. Dogs bow, chimpanzees wear a loose open-mouthed face, and rats give a high call before wrestling. These signals matter to the definition, because without them a play fight and a real fight look the same to an observer with a notebook.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The oldest explanation is practice. On this account a young predator that stalks its sibling is rehearsing the movements it will need to hunt, and a young deer that runs and turns is training the muscles and reflexes that will one day outrun a wolf. The idea is attractive and the evidence for it is weaker than most people assume. Several studies have failed to find any link between how much an individual played as a juvenile and how well it hunted as an adult, and cats raised without the chance to chase objects still hunt competently. Practice may be part of the story, but it does not carry it alone.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A second explanation says that play builds brains rather than skills. Rats deprived of rough-and-tumble play as juveniles grow up with measurable differences in the prefrontal cortex, the region that handles flexible responses to unexpected situations, and they behave accordingly: put into a social situation they have not met before, they are slower to work out what is expected and more likely to respond with aggression. On this view the function of play is not to rehearse any particular action but to build a nervous system that copes with surprise, which is why play so often involves deliberately putting yourself off balance.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A third explanation is social. In species that live in groups, play is where the young learn what the group will tolerate. A rat that bites too hard during wrestling finds that its partner refuses the next invitation, and young animals that play with everyone in a litter are, in some studies, better at forming alliances later. There is an intriguing pattern in the data: in several species the stronger partner routinely handicaps itself, letting the smaller animal win a fair share of the bouts, which suggests that keeping the game going matters more to both of them than winning it.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: These accounts are usually presented as rivals, and they need not be. Play is not one behaviour: chasing, wrestling, object manipulation and solitary acrobatics differ in who does them, when they peak and what they cost, and it would be surprising if a single function explained all of them. Comparative work suggests that the species which play most are those with long childhoods, flexible diets and complicated social lives, which is the profile of an animal whose adult problems cannot be specified in advance. Whatever else play does, it seems to be what unpredictable animals do with a protected childhood.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The uncomfortable implication is for us. Human childhood has been steadily rearranged over three generations: unsupervised outdoor play has shrunk, the school day has lengthened and adults now organise most of what children do together. Work on other species does not tell us what follows from that, and anyone who says it does is overreaching. What it does supply is a reason to take the change seriously rather than treating play as the part of childhood that can be cut when the timetable is full. In every other species that has been studied properly, the young animals that are prevented from playing grow up subtly different from the ones that are not.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The five-day week is not a law of nature. It was assembled in the first third of the twentieth century out of union pressure, factory arithmetic and one famous decision by a car manufacturer who concluded that rested workers made fewer mistakes and bought more cars. Nothing about it was calculated for an economy in which most people sit at a screen. The recent interest in a four-day week rests on a claim that sounds implausible and is at least partly measurable: that an organisation can cut a day from the week, keep pay unchanged, and lose nothing it was actually selling. Four people who have spent the past few years inside that claim disagree about almost everything except that the question is now worth asking properly.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Priya Raman has coordinated some of the largest coordinated trials, in which dozens of firms shortened the week together and reported against agreed measures. The headline results have been consistent across countries: most participating companies keep the arrangement after the trial ends, reported revenue holds steady or rises slightly, and staff turnover and sickness absence fall sharply. She is careful about what this shows. Firms that volunteer for such a trial are not a random sample; they tend to be small, to work in services, and to be run by people who already suspected the answer. What the trials demonstrate, she argues, is that the thing is possible in a real organisation, not that it would work everywhere. The distinction sounds pedantic until a government tries to write it into law.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Daniel Osei thinks the measured gains are mostly a story about meetings. When a week loses a fifth of its hours, the first casualties are the activities nobody could defend: the status meeting that could have been a message, the report that was read by no one, the approval step added after an incident in 2016. Firms in the trials cut meeting time substantially, shortened those that remained and made attendance optional, and the day disappeared without the work following it. His conclusion is deflating for both camps: the four-day week is a device for forcing a conversation about wasted time, and an organisation that held that conversation honestly could keep five days and get the same benefit.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Lena Fischer’s objection is about who is being described. Almost all the evidence comes from offices, where output is loosely defined and an hour saved can be given back. A ward, a classroom, a bus route and a warehouse do not work that way: fewer hours means fewer shifts covered, and covering them means hiring, which is a straightforward increase in cost rather than a productivity gain. Trials in such settings have generally needed extra staff and public money to work at all. A policy that improves life in software companies and leaves nurses where they were is not a shorter working week, she argues; it is a benefit for people who already have the most control over their time. Her preferred measure is blunt: count the hours of the lowest-paid worker in the organisation before and after.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Marcus Hale watches what happens to the hours themselves. In several trials the reduction in scheduled time was partly recovered outside it: people answered messages on the day off, started earlier, or compressed the same work into four longer days and reported being more tired at the end of them. Where the shortened week was genuine, he notes, it was because management removed work rather than redistributing it — and management is rarely willing to say out loud which tasks are being dropped. The gap between a four-day week and a four-day timetable is, in his data, the single best predictor of whether staff still like the arrangement a year later. A timetable can be announced in a morning; removing work takes a season and an argument.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: It is too early to be confident and too late to dismiss it. The trials are real, the effects on health and retention are among the most consistent findings in this literature, and enough firms have kept the arrangement without visible damage to make the older certainty untenable. But the evidence is drawn from self-selected organisations in a narrow band of industries, the long-run effect on careers and promotion is unmeasured, and nobody has shown what happens in a downturn, when the same firms are deciding between hours and jobs. The sensible position is that the question has moved from whether it can work anywhere to where, and at whose expense, it works.
paragraphs.label: F
